newsitem.title: USA: Florida board OKs Miami five-year budget blueprint.
newsitem.headline: Florida board OKs Miami five-year budget blueprint.

text.p: A Florida oversight board on Monday unanimously approved a Miami budget blueprint designed to keep the city operating in the black until 2002.
"We're now on a track for a great happy ending for the city of Miami," Lt. Gov. Buddy MacKay said.

MacKay has chaired the state oversight board since it was appointed by Gov. Lawton Chiles in December to force Miami to eliminate a $68 million deficit. He resigned the post after the five-year plan was approved.
"This is the right time for me to move on," MacKay said. "The hands-on part is done."
He said the board's role would shift from direct supervision to that of a review panel, "making sure they did what they said they were going to do."
The former vice chairman of the board, NationsBank Miami President Adolfo Henriques, was appointed chairman.

The five-year plan relies on a new fire district tax, operating efficiencies and cuts in benefits and services to balance the budget. It lays out plans for public-private development that is expected to increase property tax revenues.
It also leaves open the possiblity of privatizing the city's solid waste department, which has long been subsidized with general fund revenues.

The plan projects annual recurring revenues of $416.9 million in 1997 to $424.8 million in 2001. It projects surpluses of up to $1.9 million a year and replenishes the city's reserves, which were depleted to pay operating costs.
"I think that the bond market's going to respond positively to this," MacKay said.
Moody's Investors Service Inc and Standard & Poor's Corp have both cut Miami's general obligation bond rating to junk status because of the deficits.

Under the original agreement with the oversight board, Miami will remain under state supervision for three more years once it completes two years without a deficit. MacKay said the period could be shortened "if it becomes clear that this board is not needed."
The city's next big hurdle comes on Sept 4 in a referendum allowing voters to decide whether to dissolve the city and merge it into the Dade County government.
Before the budget was approved, a KPMG Peat Marwick official briefed the board on the outside audit the firm expects to finish in the next couple weeks.
Ken Deon of Peat Marwick said the audit confirms city officials' calculation that Miami had a $22 million operating deficit for fiscal 1996, which ended Sept 30, 1996.
Deon said the auditor's opinion was still pending, but would warn that Miami still has liquidity problems. Other than that, he said, "It's basically a clean bill of health."
The audit will include a letter from the bond firm of Hawkins Delafield & Wood concluding that Miami did not violate any bond covenents.

That had been in question because the city moved money between restricted and unrestricted accounts in order to pay its bills. Assistant City Manager Bob Nachlinger said city officials went over the accounts with the firm's attorneys, who concluded there was no misappropriation of bond proceeds.
